title: LIBYA: Political prisoners in Abu Salim Prison, Tripoli (UA 188/96)
summary: Urgent action about political prisoners in Abu Salim Prison, Tripoli, after a reported mutiny said to have begun around 5 July 1996 and lasted about a week. Amnesty reports that prisoners complained of poor medical care, hygiene, overcrowding and food, and held guards hostage. Special security forces reportedly stormed the prison and fired on prisoners and hostages, killing scores. Amnesty had written to Gaddafi asking for an impartial inquiry and had no reply. It asked for the names of the dead to be published and for access to doctors, lawyers and families.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: LIBYA: Amnesty International calls for an independent investigation and urges against the use of the death penalty
summary: Amnesty news release urging Gaddafi to order a prompt, impartial inquiry into the killings of many political prisoners at Abu Salim Prison, Tripoli, in early July 1996, and to publish the names of the dead. It repeats reports of a week-long mutiny over medical care, sanitation, overcrowding and food, followed by a storming by special security forces. It also reports that on 16 July 1996 Libyan television announced new capital offences (profiteering in wartime or blockade, drug, alcohol and currency offences), published in the gazette on 15 July. Note the date discrepancy with Human Rights Watch, which places the Abu Salim killings on 28-30 June 1996.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libya: Further information on political detention
collection: AI Index MDE 19/03/92 (date inferred from content; not printed on the page)
summary: Amnesty says it knows of at least 554 political prisoners in Libya, including 127 names not previously published, and details 30 cases. At least 14 of the 15 prisoners in Appendix I are believed held at Abu Salim detention centre on the outskirts of Tripoli, as are most people arrested after the May 1984 Bab al-Aziziya attack claimed by the NFSL. Cases include Tripoli university staff and students, and a Tripoli Postal Service employee. It reports torture methods (falaqa, electric shocks, mock executions) and says Abu Salim prisoners before 1986 lacked proper medical care. It notes the March 1988 release of 400 prisoners while about 100 were excluded.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: LIBYA: Amnesty International completes first fact-finding visit in over five years
summary: Amnesty reports on a 15-23 May 2009 visit invited by the Gaddafi Foundation. Delegates visited prisoners at Jdeida (run by the General People's Committee of Justice), and at Ain Zara and Abu Salim prisons (apparently under Public Security), but were refused access to other prisoners and to relatives of the disappeared in Benghazi. It raises the Internal Security Agency's incommunicado detention and the State Security Court created in 2007. It notes the reported 10 May 2009 suicide of Ibn al-Shaykh al-Libi at Abu Salim, with no autopsy access, and the death in Amman of Fathi el-Jahmi, who had been held at Tripoli Medical Centre.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libya: 30 years on - time for action
summary: Marking 30 years of Gaddafi rule, Amnesty says hundreds of political prisoners are held without charge or trial, some for over a decade, and that torture, deaths in custody and disappearances continue. It names al-Wafi Nbiyya (sentenced after the 1993 Misrata army rebellion) and Mohammad Ali Bakoush (held without trial since February 1989) as having died in Abu Salim prison, Tripoli, in July or August 1999. It also says five prisoners of conscience convicted in 1973 over the Islamic Liberation Party were reportedly still serving life terms there. It criticises the 1997 Charter of Honour, which allows collective punishment. Embargoed until 31 August 1999.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libya: Amnesty International's prisoner concerns in the light of recent legal reforms
summary: Amnesty states that despite the March 1988 amnesty of 400 political prisoners and later legal reforms, at least 467 political prisoners remained held (details on 427), some possibly prisoners of conscience; the catalogue page gives the date 31 May 1991. The full text (a separate PDF copy) lists Tripoli detention places: Abu Salim Prison, Tripoli Central Prison, Judayda prison, a Tripoli military prison and a hospital on al-Zawiya Street. It says 392 people arrested January 1989-April 1990 were reportedly held incommunicado, at least 211 of them in Tripoli and nearby towns after demonstrations at al-Fatih University. It criticises the retained Permanent Revolutionary Court.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: LIBYA: Six men, names not known to Amnesty International (UA 352/92)
summary: Urgent action after Libyan television announced on 10 November 1992 that six men convicted of offences including rape and murder were executed that morning. Amnesty calls these the first officially announced executions in over five years; the previous announced ones were nine people convicted of politically motivated crimes in February 1987. It outlines the review chain through the Court of Cassation and the General People's Congress secretariat, and recalls Gaddafi's March 1988 call for abolition. Appeals were addressed to officials in Tripoli.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Amnesty International Newsletter, May 1977 (Libya: first executions in 23 years)
summary: Monthly newsletter whose Libya item reports that army officers were executed by firing squad on 2 April 1977, that of 75 tried in December 1976 23 were sentenced to death and the figure rose to 45 on appeal, and that five people were publicly hanged in Benghazi on 7 April. Amnesty cabled Gaddafi on 12 April. The Libya items place the hangings in Benghazi, not Tripoli; the entry is kept as 1977 context. The issue also covers many other countries.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libya: Serious human rights violations amid secrecy and isolation (report: Gross human rights violations amid secrecy and isolation)
summary: Release accompanying a 36-page report saying Libya practices arbitrary arrest, torture, extrajudicial killing and enforced disappearance with impunity. It describes the March 1997 Charter of Honour allowing collective punishment, and hostage-taking of relatives. Rashid 'Abd al-Hamid al-'Urfia, arrested February 1982, is reported still held without charge in Abu Salim Prison, Tripoli; torture is said to occur in underground rooms of Abu Salim, including electric shocks and 'car torture'. Mansur Kikhiya disappeared from Cairo in December 1993.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libya: Evidence Suggests Khamis Brigade Killed 45 Detainees
summary: HRW reports that the Khamis Brigade (32nd Brigade) appears to have shot and grenaded detainees on 23 August 2011 in a warehouse in Khalida Ferjan, Salahaddin, south of Tripoli beside the Yarmouk military base; it was burned three days later. On 27 August HRW counted about 45 bodies in the ashes. A survivor said 153 names were read at roll call, about 20 escaped, and roughly 125 detainees were civilians. A former detainee described 60-80 held at once with one litre of water a day. HRW says murder of detainees is a war crime.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libya: Gaddafi Forces Suspected of Executing Detainees
summary: HRW says forces loyal to Gaddafi probably killed at least 17 detainees around 21 August 2011 in the Al-Amal al-Akhdar building of the Internal Security service, near Gargur, Tripoli, with 17 bodies taken to Matiga hospital on 24 August. On 26 August it inspected 18 bodies in a dry riverbed between Gargur and Bab al-Aziziya and 29 more at a field clinic outside Bab al-Aziziya. It also describes checkpoint killings. HRW had not yet identified those responsible and no forensic analysis was complete.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libya: Words to Deeds - The Urgent Need for Human Rights Reform
summary: 84-page report based on HRW's first Libya visit in April-May 2005, with access to five prisons and 32 prisoners interviewed privately; 15 said they were tortured. It notes Law 71 (1972) banning group activity, the abolition of the People's Court in January 2005, 12,860 prisoners in 34 facilities in April 2005, and that all 131 prisoners a committee recommended releasing were still held on 10 January 2006. Tripoli sites: Abu Salim (June 1996 deaths, October 2005 protest by 135 People's Court prisoners), Jdeida (about 180 death-row prisoners reported), the Police Academy (Brotherhood retrial) and Mitiga airport (former Wheelus Air Base).
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libya: June 1996 Killings at Abu Salim Prison
summary: HRW compiles witness accounts of the killing of prisoners at Abu Salim prison, Tripoli, on 28-30 June 1996. Libyan groups abroad put deaths up to about 1,200 of 1,600-1,700 held. It reports that security forces fired and threw grenades on 29 June and that bodies were reportedly buried in trenches. Since 2001 authorities reportedly told 112 families of deaths; 238 families said they had lost contact. Gaddafi acknowledged killings in April 2004. HRW stresses it could not independently verify the accounts.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Amnesty International Report: Libya (annual report chapter, 'Libya 2010' edition)
source: Amnesty International (hosted by Amnesty International USA)
collection: Amnesty International annual report country entries (edition covers events of 2009; publication date on the page is unreliable)
summary: Annual entry recording that hundreds of prisoners were believed killed at Abu Salim in 1996, that authorities named a judge in September 2009 to investigate without disclosing the mandate, and that in October they announced plans to demolish the prison, which families feared would destroy evidence. Three members of a victims' families committee were arrested in March and freed days later. It notes the death of Fathi el-Jahmi, reported suicide of Ibn al-Shaykh al-Libi at Abu Salim on 9 May and the Internal Security Agency's impunity.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Amnesty International Report: Libya (annual report chapter, 'Libya 2011' edition)
source: Amnesty International (hosted by Amnesty International USA)
collection: Amnesty International annual report country entries (edition covers events of 2010; publication date on the page is unreliable)
summary: Entry stating that at least 18 executions were reported (many of foreign nationals), over 200 people were reported on death row, and the government disclosed no findings on the 1996 Abu Salim killings and rejected a UN recommendation to disclose victims' names. It reports over 200 prisoners freed in March under a 'reconciliation' framework, over 200 still arbitrarily held at year-end, and migrants detained indefinitely under Law No. 19 of 2010. Benghazi families suspended weekly protests in October after promises of assistance.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Amnesty International Report 1994 - Libya
collection: Amnesty International annual report country entries (events of 1993)
summary: Entry saying five prisoners of conscience from the banned Islamic Liberation Party (arrested 1973) were serving life terms in Abu Salim Prison, along with 17 other political prisoners after unfair trials. It reports a police sergeant-major believed held in a secret centre in the al-Hawwari district and a student held in Abu Salim, over 500 political suspects held without charge at end-1993, and arrests of scores of officers after an alleged October revolt in Misrata and Bani Walid. Mansur Kikhiya disappeared in Cairo in December 1993.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Twenty-first report of the Prosecutor of the ICC to the UN Security Council pursuant to Resolution 1970 (2011)
source: International Criminal Court, Office of the Prosecutor
collection: ICC OTP reports to the UN Security Council on Libya
summary: Report stating three ICC warrants remained outstanding (Al-Werfalli, reportedly killed 24 March 2021; Al-Tuhamy Mohamed Khaled, reportedly dead in Cairo; and Saif al-Islam Gaddafi, a 'wilful fugitive'). It alleges large-scale torture, sexual violence and arbitrary detention at Mitiga Prison, run by the Special Deterrence Force, and reports over 100 bodies recovered at Tarhuna graves since June 2020. It states over 8,850 people were arbitrarily detained in 28 official prisons and about 10,000 more in militia-run sites.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Twentieth Report of the Prosecutor of the ICC to the UN Security Council pursuant to Resolution 1970 (2011)
source: International Criminal Court, Office of the Prosecutor
collection: ICC OTP reports to the UN Security Council on Libya
summary: Describes the LNA offensive on Tripoli and a type and quantity of mines in southern Tripoli not previously seen in Libya, with 49 people killed and about 93 injured by mines between late May and early July 2020. It links Mitiga Prison to arbitrary detention, inhumane conditions and torture and asks for access for observers. It reports more than 100 bodies from mass graves in Tarhuna and southern Tripoli, and force used against protesters in Tripoli and Zawiya on 23 August 2020.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Views of the Human Rights Committee, Communication No. 1422/2005, El Hassy v. Libyan Arab Jamahiriya (CCPR/C/91/D/1422/2005)
collection: Individual communications under the Optional Protocol (views adopted 24 October 2007; copy at ICAED)
summary: The Committee found Libya violated the Covenant in the case of Abu Bakar El Hassy, held in Abu Salim prison in Tripoli from 1995 without charge, beaten, kept in the Military Unit and later the Central Unit, and unaccounted for since the June 1996 storming by special forces. Violations of Articles 7, 9, 10(1) and 2(3) were found; Libya did not respond. It asked for an investigation, return of remains if he is dead, compensation and prosecution within 180 days.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Salem Saad Ali Bashasha v. The Libyan Arab Jamahiriya (CCPR/C/100/D/1776/2008)
collection: Individual communications under the Optional Protocol (views adopted 20 October 2010; University of Minnesota Human Rights Library)
summary: Case of Milhoud Bashasha, arrested in Benghazi in October 1989 and believed held at Abu Salim near Tripoli, where family food parcels were accepted but visits refused. A death certificate issued in April 2008 and given to the family in June 2009 gave 18 June 1996 in Tripoli as the date of death, cause unknown. The Committee found violations of Articles 6, 7, 9, 10(1) and 2(3) and asked Libya to investigate, return remains, prosecute and compensate within 180 days.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Four men held incommunicado in Libya (Urgent Action 104/11)
summary: Four men, including two UK-national brothers working for a software company, were arrested on 19 March 2011 in western Tripoli by men believed to be Internal Security Agency officials, who searched the house for about four hours and took computers and documents. Relatives could not learn where they were held. Amnesty also records that about 150 people were detained at a mosque on Mizran Street, Tripoli, on 4 March 2011 to stop a planned peaceful protest. It fears torture and asks for their whereabouts to be revealed.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Journalists Detained and at Risk in Libya (Urgent Action 82/11)
summary: Concerns four Al Jazeera journalists detained near Zantan about two weeks earlier; one, Lutfi Al-Massoudi, was believed seen at a Tripoli detention centre by a CNN correspondent released on 19 March, though Tripoli authorities gave no information. It lists abuse reported by three BBC journalists (detained 7-9 March, beaten, mock executions) and four New York Times journalists, and the killing of cameraman Hassan Al Jaber on 12 March. Appeals went to Gaddafi and Musa Kusa in Tripoli.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Syrian journalist and brother held in Libya (Urgent Action 101/11)
summary: At 3am on 28 March 2011 gunmen in civilian dress raided a Tripoli home and took Syrian journalist Rana al-Aqbani, 28, and her brother Hani, who are held incommunicado. Her family learned of the arrest from Libyan state television footage of an interrogation-style interview in which she was accused of communicating with 'enemy bodies'. She worked for the Libya Press agency, closed in December 2010 after about 22 journalists were briefly detained in November 2010, and later for the state Al-Shams newspaper.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libya: Gaddafi Son Speaks From Jail
summary: HRW met Saadi Gaddafi and three other detainees at al-Hadba prison in Tripoli on 15 September 2015. Saadi said he was kept in solitary confinement and lacked legal representation from his March 2014 extradition through pretrial. It reports the 28 July 2015 trial outcome (six sentenced to death per HRW's count, 23 jailed, 37 original co-defendants), defence access to only three sessions, and an investigation into ill-treatment at al-Hadba with three former staff subject to arrest warrants. A car bomb exploded outside al-Hadba's wall on 9 September 2015.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libya: Allegations of torture of As-Saadi al-Gaddafi and two others must be thoroughly investigated
summary: Amnesty urges investigation after videos released on 3, 19 and 20 August 2015 showed abuse of As-Saadi al-Gaddafi and others at al-Hadba prison in Tripoli, apparently to force confessions, plus threats of further beatings and sexual violence. It says al-Hadba was controlled by a former Deputy Minister of Defence allied with Libya Dawn. The General Prosecutor announced an investigation on 3 August; Amnesty had no reply to its 5 August letter and notes Law 10 of 2013 sets a five-year minimum for torture to force confessions.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Abuse Behind Bars: Arbitrary and unlawful detention in Libya
summary: Documents prolonged unlawful detention by armed groups. Tripoli sites named: Mitiga airbase (Special Deterrence Force; about 2,600 held late November 2017), Abu Salim (held by the Central Security/Abu Salim group), al-Hadba (161 detainees on 17 May 2017, including 77 linked to the 1996 Abu Salim killings, who were moved and confirmed at Ain Zara in November 2017) and al-Jdeida women's prison. About 6,500 were held in 26 official prisons in October 2017, and 37 bodies with signs of torture reached Tripoli hospitals in 2017.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: UNSMIL supports Libyan efforts to align prisons with international standards
summary: Describes two Tripoli workshops (1-2 and 4-5 December 2024) on prison reform with officials, academics, Judicial Police and prosecutors, following Human Rights Council resolution A/HRC/56/70 of 3 June 2024. Participants urged amending legislation, enforcing existing laws and creating an independent national mechanism to protect people in detention. No specific facility is named.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libya - At least 250 people disappeared, 70 dead in Al Jabl Al Akhdar region
summary: Alkarama reports at least 70 deaths and 250 disappearances in eastern Libya after 16 February 2011. For Tripoli, informal sources said 10 people seized at al-Abrak airport and about 250 other abductees might be held at Al Maitiga Air Force base, reportedly controlled by the Khamis Brigade, and that about 400 Air Force Academy students were confined there from 17 February, two reportedly shot dead trying to escape. These are unverified claims by an advocacy group.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Law No. (29) of 2013 on Transitional Justice
summary: Issued in Tripoli 2 December 2013 (no gazette issue given). It covers serious rights abuses by former-regime bodies from 1 September 1969, creates an independent Fact-Finding and Reconciliation Commission with investigative powers, sets reparations through a Victims' Compensation Fund, lifts limitation periods for certain political and security crimes, and requires ministers to end detention of former-regime suspects within 90 days by prosecution or release. Refusing to cooperate with the Commission is punishable by up to six months or a fine of 1,000 dinars. It repeals Law 17 of 2012.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Cabinet Decree No. (89) of 2013 on the establishment of the General Authority for the Search and Identification of Missing Persons
summary: Creates a public authority headquartered in Tripoli to search for and identify missing persons in Libya from 1969, keep an electronic registry, collect DNA from remains and relatives, work with the public prosecution on exhumations and documenting violations, and hold unidentified remains until identification. It has a five-member board, may hire foreign experts and is audited by the Court of Accounts. No gazette issue is given. This is the legal basis of the body later reporting on Abu Salim graves.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Law No. (1) of 2014 on Assistance to Families of February 17 Revolution Martyrs and Missing Persons
summary: Issued in Tripoli 9 January 2014. It sets benefits for families of those killed or missing between 15 February and 23 October 2011: a monthly allowance, medical insurance, jobs and loan priority, a gold medal and commemorations. It creates a General Commission for the Search and Identification of Missing Persons under the Cabinet and a central verification committee, and punishes false claims with up to five years. It excludes anyone proven to have opposed the revolution. No gazette issue is given.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Law No. 10 of 2013 on the Criminalization of Torture, Forced Disappearance and Discrimination
source: Watchlist on Children and Armed Conflict (description of Libyan law)
collection: Watchlist legal resources (exact enactment date not shown)
summary: The page describes Libya's 2013 law that made enforced disappearance a crime and filled Penal Code gaps on torture (Amnesty cites a five-year minimum sentence for torture to force confessions). It says the law falls short of international standards because it does not adopt the conventions' definitions of torture and enforced disappearance. The page gives no full text or article numbers.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libya: In Repressive Atmosphere, Pockets of Improvement
collection: News releases, Libya 2009 (78-page report from a 10-day April 2009 visit)
summary: HRW presented its findings at a Tripoli news conference and met the Tripoli Bar Association and Journalists' Syndicate. It says about 500 prisoners were still held by the Internal Security Agency after serving sentences or acquittal, and that Abu Salim and Ain Zara prisons are under the agency's full control. On the 1996 Abu Salim killings (about 1,200 dead, per HRW), it notes offers of up to 200,000 dinars to families who drop claims and a seven-judge investigation panel formed in September 2009. It also reports up to 30 unresolved disappearance cases.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libya: 1996 Prison Killings Need Independent Inquiry
summary: HRW calls for an independent inquiry into the 28-29 June 1996 killings at Abu Salim prison, Tripoli. A former kitchen worker estimated up to 1,200 killed from meal counts, and said prisoners revolted on 28 June, killing a guard, before security forces fired on courtyards the next day. HRW could not verify the toll. The government had acknowledged killings, and the internal security chief said in May 2005 that an inquiry was open and that over 400 prisoners escaped in four break-outs. A Swiss-based group counted 112 families notified of deaths and 238 who had lost contact.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Concluding Observations of the Human Rights Committee: Libyan Arab Jamahiriya (CCPR/C/79/Add.101)
collection: UN treaty body concluding observations (mirrored by University of Minnesota Human Rights Library)
summary: Concluding observations adopted 2 November 1998 after the third periodic report was considered on 27 October 1998. The Committee expresses concern about reported extrajudicial killings, arbitrary arrest and prolonged detention without trial, vague death-penalty provisions, torture, flogging and amputation, and the 1997 Charter of Honour permitting collective punishment. It also questions judicial independence, long remand periods, the Revolutionary Security Courts, and press limits under the 1972 Publication Act. It does not name Tripoli places.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Al-Senussi case: Appeals Chamber confirms case is inadmissible before ICC
collection: ICC press releases, Situation in Libya
summary: ICC Appeals Chamber unanimously upheld the October 2013 finding that the case against Abdullah Al-Senussi is inadmissible because Libya is genuinely prosecuting him. The ICC warrant (27 June 2011) alleged murder and persecution as crimes against humanity committed through state forces across Libya from 15 to 28 February 2011. Libya had challenged admissibility on 2 April 2013. The release does not mention Tripoli sites.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: UN report documents horrors faced by thousands held in arbitrary detention in Libya
summary: UN News summarises an OHCHR/UNSMIL report saying armed groups across Libya hold thousands in arbitrary detention with torture and other abuse, often based on tribe, family or perceived politics. About 6,500 people were in official prisons, with thousands more in nominally state or militia-run facilities, one large western facility holding about 2,600. The news item names no specific Tripoli facility; the exact day is not shown in the extract.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Torture and arbitrary detention widespread across Libyan prisons: UN
summary: Reports the UN finding that torture is common in Libyan detention, including facilities linked to the UN-backed government. It says Mitiga facility, at the Tripoli airbase and run by the Special Deterrence Force (Rada), held 2,600 detainees at end of November 2017 according to the prosecutor general's office, and notes about 6,500 in official prisons. Abu Salim jail is mentioned only in a photo caption about a mural.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Law on Prisons (Law No. 19 of 1962)
summary: Monarchy-era prisons law issued by King Idris I (1 May 1962; no gazette issue number in the translation). It sets principal, central and special prisons, written admission orders, a separation of Category A prisoners (including political offenders) from others, and doctors, visits, discipline and judicial inspection. It limits firearm use by guards. It was repealed by Law 47 of 1975, so it is the baseline regime inherited in 1969.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Law No. (87) of 1974 adding certain provisions to the Code of Criminal Procedure
summary: RCC law of 20 November 1974 for offences against state security (Penal Code Book 2, Part 1). Arrestees must be brought before the Public Prosecution within seven days; the Prosecution holds the powers of the investigating magistrate and indictment chamber; initial detention orders run 15 days, extendable once, then by court in 45-day periods. Defence counsel is appointed by the Court of Appeal head. No gazette number is given in the translation.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Law No. (47) of 1975 on Prisons
summary: Replaced the 1962 prisons law. It defines prisons as places of reform, requires a written prosecution order for detention, segregates inmates by category and sex, mandates work, education and a doctor in each prison, regulates visits and discipline (restraints generally limited to 72 hours), allows firearms only after a warning shot, and sets procedures for executions. Prosecutors may inspect prisons. No gazette issue is given.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Law No. (50) of 2012 on Compensation of Political Prisoners
source: Interim National Transitional Council (via DCAF security-legislation.ly)
summary: Issued in Tripoli, this law covers civilians and military personnel held in prisons or special detention camps between 1 September 1969 and 15 February 2011 for opposing the former regime. It sets compensation of 8,000 dinars a month of detention, deducts sums already paid, and revokes the convictions concerned. The Cabinet was to issue implementing rules.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Law No. (61) of 2012 amending Law No. (38) of 2012 Establishing Some Provisions of the Transitional Phase
source: Interim National Transitional Council (via DCAF security-legislation.ly)
summary: Issued in Tripoli on 31 July 2012, it amends Article 1 of Law 38/2012 to require the Interior and Defence ministers to refer detained former-regime senior officials to prosecutors where evidence exists, and otherwise release them no later than 30 August 2012. It shows how the interim authorities tried to put revolutionary detention under legal process.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Law No. (3) of 2013 on the Amendment of the Code of Criminal Procedure
summary: Adopted 12 February 2013 and issued in Tripoli 24 February 2013. It amends Arts. 187 bis (A) and (B): arrestees go to the Public Prosecution within seven days, are questioned within three days, prosecution detention orders last two weeks, and a judge may extend in 45-day periods. It updates the 1974 regime for state-security offences.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Cabinet Decree No. (513) of 2013 issuing the Executive Regulation for Law No. (50) of 2012 on compensation of political prisoners
summary: Implementing regulation for the 2012 compensation law. Eligibility is checked against records of four former bodies: Internal Security, External Security, Intelligence and Military Police. Applicants lacking records may use a sworn statement with two witnesses over 40, ideally former inmates of the same facility. It excludes espionage, illegal immigration, rioting and sports-demonstration cases, and caps instalments at 300,000 dinars.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Law No. (9) of 2014 amending Law No. (29) of 2013 on transitional justice
summary: Issued in Tripoli 24 March 2014. It amends Article 26 of the transitional justice law, directing the Justice, Interior and Defence ministries to end within 120 days the detention of people accused of crimes under the former regime, either by referral to prosecution where evidence exists or by release. Referral does not itself invalidate earlier detention.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libya: Halt Exhumations of Mass Graves
summary: HRW urges the NTC to stop ad hoc exhumations until forensic experts are present. A tractor driver told HRW he buried several hundred bodies from across Tripoli at a cemetery around 20 August 2011. ICRC reportedly handled 125 bodies from 12 sites, and new mass graves were found weekly. HRW warns that graves of an estimated 1,200 prisoners killed in the 1996 Abu Salim massacre are at risk.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libya: Use Forensic Experts to Exhume Prison Grave
summary: HRW says a reported Tripoli grave may hold about 1,200 prisoners killed in June 1996 at Abu Salim. The provisional government said on 25 September 2011 that it was in a field outside the prison wall; HRW could not confirm the exact spot. It asks for the site to be guarded and for a moratorium until forensic experts arrive, noting the ICRC has only two forensic experts and does not gather legal evidence.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libya: Investigate unidentified bodies and reported mass graves in Abu Salim
summary: ICJ urges investigation after fighting in May 2025 following the 12 May killing of SSA head Abdelghani al-Kikli. It says the General Authority for the Search and Identification of Missing Persons (established 2018) reported on 15 May information on mass graves at the Abu Salim zoo, and the Interior Ministry reported 50 more unidentified bodies in the Abu Salim hospital morgue on 19 May. As of 27 May no public prosecutor investigation had been announced; the exact body count differs between sources.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Press Statement on the discovery of several mass graves and unidentified bodies in the locality of Abu Salim, Tripoli
source: African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights
summary: Dated Banjul 29 May 2025 (posted 31 May). The Commission voices concern at reports of several mass graves in Abu Salim, an area previously controlled by the al-Kikli militia. It cites 9 unidentified bodies in Alkhdra hospital morgue and more than 50 at Alhawadith hospital, plus the missing-persons authority's information about graves in the Abu Salim zoo. It calls for prompt, independent investigation.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Abu Salim killings perpetrators identified, says Attorney General
summary: Reports that at least ten men were killed in a house in Abu Salim, Tripoli, on 17 February 2024. The Interior Minister promised accountability; on 24 February the Attorney General's Office said perpetrators were identified and arrest warrants issued, leaving arrests to the Tripoli Security Directorate. On 26 February four arrests were ordered, including a relative of Stability Support Agency commander al-Kikli (as reported). Unrelated to the 1996 case, it shows recent violence in the same district.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libyan court passes jail massacre case to military tribunals
summary: AFP reports a Tripoli court declined to rule on the 1996 Abu Salim prison massacre and transferred it to a military tribunal, calling it a case of 'military character'. It had been before a Tripoli appeals court since May 2021 after the Supreme Court overturned a 2019 inadmissibility ruling. AFP gives 1,269 inmates killed in 1996; named main suspects are Abdullah al-Senussi and Mansour Daou.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Qadhafi's intelligence chief al-Senussi acquitted in 2011 crackdown case
summary: Reports that on 18 May 2026 the Tripoli Court of Appeal acquitted Abdullah al-Senussi of all charges in the 2011 crackdown case (No. 630), with lawyer Ahmed Nashad saying the ruling also cleared Mansour Dhao and Saif al-Islam Qadhafi. Al-Senussi faced about 26 charges and had not been released. The separate Abu Salim 1996 case reportedly remained under review without final judgment. The account rests on his lawyer and a single outlet; treat as unconfirmed pending court sources.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libya: Deadly Attack Highlights Disregard for Civilians
summary: HRW reports an airstrike on a compound in Tajoura, east of Tripoli, that killed at least 44 migrants and asylum seekers; it held at least 600 people. HRW says about 5,800 migrants were held without charge in GNA-controlled facilities, about 3,300 of them in greater Tripoli, and criticises the GNA for not evacuating centres near military sites. The GNA blamed Haftar forces, which denied responsibility.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Report of the International Commission of Inquiry on Libya (A/HRC/19/68)
collection: Commission of Inquiry on Libya (RightDocs mirror; page metadata shows a different posting date; report presented February 2012)
summary: The Commission visited more than 20 official and unofficial detention sites and interviewed 150 people. For Tripoli it records over 200 bodies at morgues on 20-21 February 2011 (according to doctors) and describes the Yarmouk warehouse beside the 32nd Brigade base, where on 23 August 2011 guards threw grenades and shot detainees; of 157 detainees only 51 survivors were confirmed. It cites 21 shot dead at the Gargur detention centre and 15 bodies near Bab al-Aziziya. It also reports torture and sexual violence against men in Abu Salim, attacks on Tawerghans in Tripoli, and about 8,000 detainees held by new authorities.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Report of the International Commission of Inquiry to investigate all alleged violations of international human rights law in the Libyan Arab Jamahiriya (A/HRC/17/44)
collection: Commission of Inquiry on Libya (RightDocs mirror; metadata lists January 2012)
summary: First report of the Commission of Inquiry. For Tripoli it describes security forces dispersing demonstrators in Green Square and Algeria Square on 17 February 2011 and larger clashes on 20-21 February, with indiscriminate force and apparent shoot-to-kill patterns. It cites HRW's count of at least 62 bodies in Tripoli morgues on 20-22 February and information on about 15 killed on 20 February in Fashloum, Tajoura and al-Dibri. Witnesses described security forces removing bodies, raiding hospitals and arresting organisers on 16 February. The Commission visited Tripoli and met 30 detainees held in Tripoli and Benghazi.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Report of the High Commissioner under Human Rights Council resolution S-15/1: Situation of human rights in the Libyan Arab Jamahiriya (A/HRC/17/45)
collection: UN Human Rights Council, 17th session (copy hosted at hrvoices.org)
summary: High Commissioner's report prepared without staff on the ground, so all allegations are unverified. Tripoli references include the reported dragging of a law student out of the Rixos hotel on 26 March 2011 after she told journalists she had been raped at a checkpoint, the government's claim that Gaddafi's son and three grandchildren died in a NATO strike in Tripoli on 30 April 2011, a migrant boat leaving Tripoli with 72 people of whom 61 reportedly died, and fuel queues. It has no dedicated Tripoli section.

title: Saif Al-Islam Gaddafi case: ICC Appeals Chamber confirms case is admissible before the ICC
collection: ICC press releases, Situation in Libya
summary: The Appeals Chamber unanimously rejected Saif Al-Islam Gaddafi's appeal, holding that his July 2015 conviction by a Tripoli court was in absentia and so not final under Libyan law, and that Libya's 2015 amnesty law (Law No. 6) did not cover the crimes charged. The release also recalls the 2011 Security Council referral, the 2011 warrants for Gaddafi and Abdullah Al-Senussi, and the later inadmissibility rulings in the Senussi case.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: 33th session of the Human Rights Council (UNSMIL press release)
summary: UNSMIL statement to the Human Rights Council. It reports that 12 prisoners released by court order from al-Ruwaimi prison in Tripoli in June 2016 were found dead about 24 hours later, beaten and shot, with perpetrators unidentified. It describes severe overcrowding at Mitiga detention facility, women guarded by men, children held with adults, and two deaths since March allegedly from torture. It notes the Tripoli-based National Council for Civil Liberties and Human Rights was effectively shut by intimidation.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Press Release: UN Report on Torture in Libya
collection: UNSMIL press releases (OHCHR/UNSMIL report 'Torture and Deaths in Detention in Libya')
summary: Datelined Tripoli. The joint report is based on visits to nearly 30 detention centres over two years. It estimates about 8,000 conflict-related detainees, mostly without due process, and 27 deaths in custody since late 2011 likely caused by torture, 11 in 2013 at brigade-run centres. It notes an April 2013 law criminalising torture and a September 2013 transitional justice law requiring detainee screening within 90 days. The release does not name specific Tripoli facilities.

title: Crimes against humanity and war crimes in Libya finally before the ICC
source: European Center for Constitutional and Human Rights (ECCHR)
collection: ECCHR case pages, ICC Libya situation
summary: ECCHR reports that on 16 July 2026 ICC Pre-Trial Chamber confirmed all 17 counts and committed Khaled Mohamed Ali El Hishri (Al Buti) to trial. He is described as a senior figure in the Tripoli militia formerly known as SDF/RADA, allegedly in post at Mitiga Prison between 1 May 2014 and 30 June 2020. Germany arrested him in Berlin on 16 July 2025 and surrendered him on 1 December 2025. Charges include torture, imprisonment, rape and sexual violence, murder, enslavement and persecution of Libyan detainees and migrants. This is an NGO account of the Court's decision.

title: Civil Society Joint Statement: Germany's surrender of El Hishri to the ICC is a turning point for accountability in the Libya Situation
source: International Commission of Jurists (joint NGO statement)
summary: Joint statement welcoming Germany's 1 December 2025 surrender of Khaled El Hishri to the ICC after his 16 July 2025 arrest in Berlin. He is alleged to hold a senior role at Mitiga Prison in Tripoli within the Special Deterrence Force (Al-Radaa). The warrant alleges crimes between 2015 and early 2020. Signatories criticise the exclusion of sub-Saharan African detainees from the charges and Italy's failure in January 2025 to surrender another suspect, Osama Elmasry Njeem.

It reports US strikes on a Libyan missile site and two patrol boats, Libya's disputed claim of three downed aircraft, and Libyan radio calls for attacks on Americans abroad. A CBS report from Tripoli described Green Square lit festively with no visible tension. It also notes that Reagan learned only afterwards of envoy William Wilson's January trip to Tripoli.

title: Libya: Gross human rights violations amid secrecy and isolation
summary: The full report describes arbitrary arrest, torture, disappearances, extrajudicial executions and unfair trials. Tripoli-area places named: Abu Salim Prison (hundreds held, some up to 15 years without charge; underground interrogation rooms beneath the administration building; a July 1996 revolt with 30-40 reported killed, after which visits were banned), Tajura Prison (businessmen held after a 1996 anti-corruption sweep), al-Jdayda Prison (24 students tortured and sentenced in 1995 after a secret trial), al-'Ataba Prison (African workers held in mid-1996) and Tripoli Central Hospital. It counts at least 38 announced executions between November 1992 and March 1997, including eight men on 2 January 1997.

title: The Battle for Libya: Killings, Disappearances and Torture
collection: Press release for a 107-page report (AI Index MDE 19/025/2011)
summary: Press release launching a 107-page report on the six-month conflict, based mainly on a fact-finding visit of 26 February to 28 May 2011 to al-Bayda, Ajdabiya, Brega, Benghazi, Misratah and Ras Lanouf, with a return in late August. title: New Libya 'stained' by detainee abuse (Libya: Detention abuses staining the new Libya)
collection: Press release and briefing (AI Index MDE 19/036/2011); publication day not shown on the page
summary: Amnesty reports that militias arrested as many as 2,500 people in Tripoli and al-Zawiya after late August 2011. Based on 11 detention facilities visited between 18 August and 21 September and about 300 detainee interviews, it found none had seen an arrest warrant, some showed clear signs of torture, and two guards admitted beating detainees to obtain confessions faster. Sub-Saharan Africans suspected of being mercenaries were a third to a half of detainees; children were held with adults. It asks the NTC to place centres under the Justice Minister.

title: Libya: Militia stranglehold corrosive for rule of law (report: Libya - rule of law or rule of militias?)
collection: Press release (exact day not shown in the extract)
summary: Issued just before the July 2012 elections, based on May-June 2012 research in Benghazi, Kufra, Nafousa, Sabha, Tripoli and al-Zawiya. Amnesty says about 4,000 detainees were held in centres outside central control, abuse was documented in 12 of 15 centres where private interviews took place, and at least 20 detainees had died in custody from torture since late August 2011. The Interior Ministry said it dismantled only four militias in Tripoli. It also cites a May 2012 law granting revolutionaries immunity and the continued exclusion of Tawergha's roughly 30,000 people.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libya: End Violent Crackdown in Tripoli
summary: HRW documents arrests and disappearances in Tripoli after the February 2011 protests, saying residents described detention of protesters, critics and people who spoke to foreign media, some reportedly tortured. Security forces opened fire on a protest in Green Square around 20 February and deployed heavily in Tajoura and Fashloum, with arrests beginning that night. Wounded protesters were reportedly seized from hospitals. Detainees were feared held at Jdeida, Ain Zara and Abu Salim prisons. It cites the detention of the Sewehli family from 28 February and three BBC journalists held for 21 hours on 7 March.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libya: Commanders Should Face Justice for Killings
summary: HRW reports witness accounts of forces firing randomly at protesters in Tripoli on 21-22 February 2011, and hospital sources saying at least 62 people were brought to two Tripoli hospitals since 20 February. It names Ben Ashour (shooting at passers-by), Abu Salim (at least 50 bodies reportedly in the hospital morgue), Green Square (12 dead taken to Central Hospital), Fashloum and Tajoura, and the 20 February break-up of a professionals' protest at the Tripoli courthouse. HRW could not independently verify the accounts.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libya: Diplomat Dies in Militia Custody
summary: HRW reports that Omar Brebesh, a 62-year-old former ambassador to France, died on 20 January 2012 less than 24 hours after going to a Zintan-based militia base in the Crimea neighbourhood of Tripoli for questioning on 19 January. Preliminary autopsy findings and photographs indicated torture, and a judicial police report reportedly gave torture as the cause of death. HRW cites the ICRC count of about 8,500 detainees in roughly 60 facilities, mostly militia-run, and called for an independent investigation.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libya: Militias Kill Unarmed Protesters
summary: HRW reports that on 15 November 2013 Misrata militias fired on a largely peaceful march called by the Tripoli Local Council against illegal armed groups, which went from al-Quds Square toward Gharghour where militias occupied villas formerly belonging to Gaddafi officials. Government figures cited 43 dead and at least 460 wounded. HRW counted 18 bodies at Abu Salim Trauma Hospital and 7 at Zawiya Street Hospital and saw armed militiamen moving freely inside both. An ambulance was fired on. A related attack on al-Fallah displaced camp on 16 November killed at least one.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libya: 6 Months On, Scant Action on Protester Killings
summary: HRW says at least 46 people were killed and about 500 injured when militias fired on the 15 November 2013 Tripoli protest, and that police and military police present did not intervene. A seven-member prosecution committee led by Omar Zinbeel was investigating 47 deaths; media reported one suspect from a Gharghour-based Misrata militia held by a Tripoli unit. It contrasts this with the lack of arrests six months after the 8 June 2013 Benghazi clash that killed 32.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libya: Bolster Security at Tawergha Camps
summary: HRW urges security for about 12,000 displaced Tawerghans in western Libya, most in Tripoli. Militias raided the Janzur camp at the Marine/Naval Academy on 6 February 2012, killing seven, including a 12-year-old girl, with no evidence of investigation. About 300 people at the Airport Road camp in Tripoli were raided twice in February, with three men detained. UNHCR counted about 35,000 displaced Tawerghans nationwide.
rights_note: Summary written for this archive; follow the link for the original.

title: Libya: Stop Revenge Crimes Against Displaced Persons
collection: News releases, Libya 2013 (satellite imagery analysis of Tawergha)
summary: HRW says forced displacement of about 40,000 Tawerghans, arbitrary detention, torture and killings may amount to crimes against humanity, and that satellite imagery shows 1,690 structures damaged or destroyed in Tawergha, over 90 percent burned. It lists four Tripoli camps (Naval Academy in Janzur, Airport Road, al-Fallah, Sarraj) with about 13,000 Tawerghans, and the 6 February 2012 Janzur raid that killed seven. It could not verify claims of up to 1,300 dead, detained or missing.

title: Conclusions and recommendations of the Committee against Torture: Libyan Arab Jamahiriya (A/54/44, paras. 176-189)
collection: UN treaty body conclusions (University of Minnesota Human Rights Library)
summary: Committee against Torture conclusions after considering Libya's third periodic report on 5, 6 and 10 May 1999 (22nd session). It says Libya's report did not answer concerns raised in 1994, warns that prolonged incommunicado detention may breach the Convention, notes continuing torture allegations, criticises extradition of persons to a state where they risked torture, and flags Penal Code Article 206 as an obstacle to independent NGOs. It does not name Tripoli places. Date given is the last meeting date.

title: Long Struggle for Truth: Enforced Disappearances in Libya
summary: Amnesty says thousands of families lack answers about relatives disappeared or killed by state agents in past decades. For Abu Salim Prison it repeats that up to 1,200 were killed in June 1996, that a committee formed in September 2009 had published nothing, and that at least 1,167 victim families were identified. It cites the 1980 case of Amer Deghayes, whose body was released from the Zawiya Hospital morgue in Tripoli with a suicide certificate, and the 2009 compensation offer of about 200,000 dinars refused by Miloud Boushasha's family. It records 37 attacks on exiles in 1980-1987, 25 fatal.

title: United Nations Finds Libya Responsible for Torture and Orders Compensation to Victim's Family (El Hassy v. Libya)

OMCT and Human Rights Solidarity represented the complainant.

title: Investigation by the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights on Libya (A/HRC/31/47)
summary: OHCHR investigation under HRC resolution 28/30 into 2014-2015, finding widespread violations by all parties, including arbitrary detention and torture. It reports about 9,000 people held in Justice and Interior ministry facilities and 6,200 in Justice Ministry facilities as of March 2014, only 10 percent sentenced after trial, and 3,245 migrants detained in western Libya in May 2015. title: Report of the High Commissioner on the human rights situation in Libya and technical assistance (A/HRC/34/42)

title: Events of 2 years ago sparked current uprising in Libya
collection: Commentary by Jo Becker (also in GlobalPost)
summary: HRW commentary tracing the 2011 uprising to the campaign by families of Abu Salim 1996 victims. It says over 1,200 prisoners were killed, with shooting lasting more than two hours, in a prison run by the Internal Security Agency. In March 2007 about 30 families filed a civil claim in the North Benghazi Court, which ruled for them but was ignored; weekly Saturday protests followed, and lawyer Fathi Terbil was detained in 2009. Officials later notified over 900 families and offered about 100,000 dollars per victim, which many refused.

title: Libya: Mark Anniversary by Restoring Rights
summary: HRW urges Gaddafi, at 40 years in power, to repeal repressive laws and free political prisoners. About 200 prisoners were reportedly held despite completed sentences or acquittal; Law 19 requires 50 founders to form an association and decision 312/2009 requires 30 days' notice for meetings. It repeats that up to 1,200 prisoners were killed at Abu Salim on 29 June 1996, and that compensation of 200,000 dinars with death certificates is not accountability. HRW interviewed a prisoner at Abu Salim in April 2009 and was denied access to another detainee.

title: Libya: Time to make human rights a reality
summary: Report on a two-week February 2004 visit, Amnesty's first in years; delegates met Gaddafi on 29 February. It cites Abu Salim Prison (director Milad Daman said requested prisoners were 'terrorist' cases), 'Ayn Zara Prison on Tripoli's outskirts (where Fathi al-Jahmi was reportedly moved during the visit) and Jdeida Prison (a detainee beaten with wire in January 2004). It reports the Muslim Brothers case (152 tried, 73 life sentences, 66 acquitted) and prolonged incommunicado detention and torture to extract confessions. It urges abolition of the People's Court and a death-penalty moratorium.

title: Libya: Towards ensuring human rights protection (initial findings of an Amnesty International visit)

title: Libya: Reforms Welcome, But Concerns Remain
summary: After HRW's first Libya mission (three weeks, five prisons, over two dozen prisoners interviewed), it says Fathi al-Jahmi had been held over 13 months without trial at an internal security facility in Tripoli since 26 March 2004, and writer Abdul Rezak al-Mansouri was held incommunicado from 12 January. It notes the People's Court was closed in 2004, two Muslim Brotherhood leaders were on death row with 84 other members imprisoned, and that a security chief said an Abu Salim investigation was open and over 400 prisoners had escaped in four episodes.

title: Libya: 202 Prisoners Released But Hundreds Still Held Arbitrarily
summary: HRW welcomes the 24 March 2010 release of at least 202 prisoners, including 80 who had been acquitted but kept in custody. Saif al-Islam al-Gaddafi announced 214 releases at a Tripoli news conference, said 409 prisoners remained in Abu Salim prison and that 232 would soon be freed. Reports said Abu Salim authorities refused to release 12 listed prisoners. In December 2009 the internal security head told HRW his agency held 330 prisoners at Abu Salim whose sentences had ended or who were acquitted.

title: Libya: Libyan Dissident, Long Imprisoned, Is Dead
summary: HRW reports that Fathi al-Jahmi, 68, died in Amman on 20 May 2009 after about six and a half years in detention for calling for a free press and elections. After his March 2004 arrest he was held at a special facility on the coast near Tripoli, sent to a psychiatric hospital in September 2006 and moved to Tripoli Medical Centre in July 2007. HRW visited him there on 25-26 April 2009, found him very weak, and he said he was not free to leave. He went into a coma on 3 May and was flown to Amman.

title: Two bodies discovered in mass grave in Abu Salim
summary: Reports that on 9 March 2026 a GNU Interior Ministry unit announced a grave in Abu Salim, Tripoli, holding two bodies, reportedly of people killed and buried by members of the now-defunct Stability Support Agency (SSA). The grave was in the al-Hadba project area, described as an SSA stronghold. Search continues with the Attorney General's Office and Criminal Investigation Department. It also says criminal groups linked to the SSA hid kidnapped, tortured and killed people there. Single-outlet account.

title: UN rights chief urges action on mass graves, abuse sites in Libya
source: Anadolu Agency (reporting UN High Commissioner Volker Turk)
summary: Reports that Volker Turk expressed shock at abuses at official and unofficial detention sites run by the Stabilization Support Apparatus in Tripoli. Between 18 and 21 May 2025 the UN received credible reports of 10 charred bodies at the SSA's Abu Salim headquarters, 67 bodies in refrigerators at Abu Salim and Al Khadra hospitals, and a burial site at the SSA-run Tripoli Zoo. title: Libya: Sites of gross human rights violations must be sealed and impartially investigated - Turk
source: UNSMIL / UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
summary: High Commissioner Volker Turk calls for sealing detention sites in Tripoli run by the Stabilization Support Apparatus. Reported 18-21 May 2025: 10 charred bodies excavated at the SSA headquarters in Abu Salim, 67 bodies in refrigerators at Abu Salim and Al Khadra hospitals (some decomposed after power outages), and a reported burial site at the SSA-run Tripoli Zoo. Forensic authorities had not been allowed to excavate. He noted the Attorney-General formed two committees and urged restraint after SSA leader al-Kikli's killing.

title: Attorney General and GNU release new details on Tripoli clashes
collection: News (reporting Attorney General's Office update of 9 July 2025)
summary: Reports that an Attorney General committee found unlawful detention at Mitiga Prison, controlled by Rada, where some detainees had unexecuted release orders. The Office confirmed 15 civilian deaths in the May 2025 fighting and five deaths in correctional centres, with 461 inmates escaping, and ordered the arrest of 172 SSA suspects on murder, kidnapping and torture charges, of whom 11 were detained. The Justice Ministry aims to bring facilities under judicial oversight.

title: Libyan appeals court clears 31 Gaddafi-era officials over 2011 protest crackdown
collection: News (exact day not shown; matches the May 2026 verdict)
summary: A Tripoli court acquitted 31 former officials, including Abdullah al-Senussi and Baghdadi al-Mahmoudi, of charges (37 counts) tied to suppressing the 2011 uprising in a case that began in 2014. Proceedings were dropped for those who died, including Saif al-Islam Gaddafi, whom the article says was killed in February. In 2015 nine were sentenced to death, 23 jailed and four acquitted before the Supreme Court overturned the convictions. Al-Senussi still faces trial over Abu Salim 1996; rights groups said the trial risked entrenching impunity.

title: ICC decision to allow Abdallah al-Senussi to stand trial in Libya 'deeply alarming' amidst overwhelming security vacuum
summary: Amnesty criticises the ICC Appeals Chamber ruling letting Libya try al-Senussi, citing about two years without a lawyer, prolonged solitary confinement and the death penalty risk. It describes the fighting between rival militias in Tripoli since 13 July 2014 around Tripoli International Airport, with at least 47 killed and more than 120 injured, damage to the airport and aircraft and to homes, mosques and a medical facility. UNSMIL staff had temporarily withdrawn, raising doubt that observers could attend the trial.

title: Saif al Islam sentenced to death - but Libyan judicial system is far from fair
summary: Reports that a Tripoli court sentenced eight Gaddafi-era officials to death, including Saif al-Islam (in absentia, held in Zintan) and Abdullah Senussi, who was convicted over the 2011 Benghazi killings, not Abu Salim. The author says former spy chief Abuzeid Dorda told the court confessions were extracted by torture and that the prison where the trial was held is controlled by a militia. The piece describes the proceedings as failing international standards.

title: World Report 2011: Libya (events of 2010)
summary: States that the Internal Security Agency controls Ain Zara and Abu Salim prisons holding political and security detainees and that about 213 people stayed jailed after sentences ended or acquittal, with judicial release orders refused. Authorities freed 214 prisoners in March 2010, including 80 of 330 held despite acquittals. It repeats the 200,000-dinar offer to Abu Salim victims' families, most Benghazi families refusing. Its only explicit Tripoli reference is the December 2009 HRW news conference in the capital, the first by an independent rights group.

title: An End to Gaddafi's Tyranny: The Liberation of the Hated Abu Salim Prison
source: Andy Worthington (blog; reprints Washington Post and CNN reports)
summary: Blog post on the opposition's takeover of Abu Salim prison in Tripoli in August 2011. It reprints a Washington Post account of roughly 2,500 detainees freed and a CNN piece on Hussein Shafei, jailed 1988-2000. It links the prison to the 1996 massacre of about 1,200 inmates and to lawyer Fathi Terbil, whose 15 February 2011 arrest in Benghazi helped trigger the uprising. title: Letter, Erich Honecker to the General Secretary of the People's Congress of the Great Socialist People's Libyan Arab Jamahiriya, Colonel Muammar al-Qaddafi (29 November 1977)
collection: Wilson Center Digital Archive (East German SED records)
summary: East German leader Honecker, for the SED Politburo, asks Qaddafi to receive Politburo member Werner Lamberz as special envoy in Tripoli on 7 or 8 December 1977. The agenda is consultations on the Horn of Africa, talks with Palestinian representatives and development of bilateral ties under agreements signed in October 1977. It shows Tripoli as a venue for Eastern-bloc diplomacy during the Jamahiriya period.

title: Stenographic Transcript of the Official Talks between Comrade Erich Honecker and Comrade Colonel Muammar al-Gaddafi in Tripoli
collection: Wilson Center Digital Archive (SAPMO-BA J IV 1857; translated by Bernd Schaefer)
summary: Transcript of talks held in Tripoli between the East German leader and Gaddafi. title: Note on Qaddafi's reaction to socialist support for Arab countries in the war in Lebanon
collection: Wilson Center Digital Archive (East German records, handwritten note by Honecker)
summary: Records that on 26 June 1982 Qaddafi met in Tripoli the heads of mission of the USSR, Bulgaria, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania and the GDR. He said Libya could not answer ordinary people asking about friendship with socialist states, derided Soviet arms purchases as 'toys', and said Libya had halted arms deals. The Soviet ambassador rejected this. The GDR embassy saw it as consistent with recent Libyan treatment of socialist diplomats.

title: National Security Decision Directive 224: Counter-Terrorist Operations Against Libya
summary: Top Secret directive citing evidence tying the 5 April 1986 West Berlin bombing to the Libyan People's Bureau in East Berlin and to Tripoli. It orders pre-emptive air strikes on terrorism-related targets in Libya no later than dawn on 15 April 1986, with efforts to limit civilian casualties and an initial exclusion of economic targets, two carrier groups to stay in the Mediterranean, and briefings of allies including the UK, France, West Germany, Italy, Spain and Canada.
